**The Whisper of Forgotten Things**

There’s a quiet magic in the things we leave behind—the half-finished books on nightstands, the keys in drawers that no longer fit any lock, the scarves tucked in coat pockets from winters we don’t remember. They’re not just clutter; they’re the echoes of selves we’ve outgrown, like shed skin or the faint scent of a perfume you once loved but can no longer name.

I think about this often when I walk through old neighborhoods. The houses seem smaller, the streets narrower, as if the world has been folding in on itself while I wasn’t looking. Maybe it’s just perspective, the way memory stretches and compresses time like taffy. Or maybe the past is a living thing, breathing in the cracks of the present. You ever notice how certain songs can yank you backward so hard it feels like falling? That’s the past, reaching out with sticky fingers.

Lately, I’ve been collecting oddities—broken watches, postcards with no messages, a single earring I found on a park bench. Not because they’re valuable, but because they feel like clues. Like if I hold enough of them, I might piece together something true. Or maybe I’m just afraid of forgetting how it felt to be someone else.

What if the things we lose aren’t gone, but just waiting in the dark, humming softly to themselves?

(Also, have you ever eaten a mango so ripe it drips down your arm like honey? That’s joy, undiluted. We should do that more often.)
